# When unidirectional tires are rotated, do they also need to be flipped?

When you rotate a set of unidirectional tires, the most critical rule is that every single tire must face the exact same direction. If one tire rotates forward and another rotates backward relative to the vehicle's travel, you will create an immediate imbalance in noise and handling characteristics. This is precisely what appears to have happened with your 2005 Subaru Outback equipped with Hankook Optimo H727s.

Unidirectional tires are engineered with a specific tread pattern designed to evacuate water efficiently in one direction. The grooves act like channels, pushing water away from the tire's center toward the outside to prevent hydroplaning and reduce road noise. Because of this specialized geometry, these tires must always be mounted so that the directional arrow on the sidewall points forward (in the direction of travel).

If a shop rotates your tires by moving them between axles but fails to flip them end-for-end, you end up with a configuration where the left side of the vehicle has one tire facing forward and the right side has a tire facing backward. While this might seem acceptable for handlingâsince the vehicle still moves forwardâthe acoustic result is disastrous. The noise profile changes drastically depending on which side of the car the tire is on because the airflow interaction with the tread pattern differs between the front-facing and rear-facing orientations.

In your specific case, the report that the noise increased significantly above 40 mph suggests a resonance issue caused by this mismatch. When tires are mounted incorrectly relative to each other, they can generate standing waves or amplify specific frequencies of road noise that cancel out when all four tires are aligned correctly. The fact that the noise started immediately after rotation confirms that the mechanical alignment of the car (suspension and steering) is likely fine, but the tire orientation is wrong.

The confusion often stems from the term "cross-rotation." For unidirectional tires, you can indeed move a tire from the front left to the rear right or vice versa, provided you flip it end-for-end so the tread still faces forward. If you simply swap FL to RR and FR to RL without flipping, you are effectively mounting two tires backward on one side of the car (if your original mount had them facing correctly) or creating a mixed orientation scenario.

To correct this, you must ensure that regardless of which axle the tire is on, the tread pattern faces forward. Visually inspecting the grooves should show that they all slope in the same direction relative to the road surface. If one side of the car has the "left side" of the tread facing outward and the other side has the "right side" facing outward, as you observed, the tires have not been flipped correctly during the rotation service.

There is no software configuration or alignment adjustment that can fix this; the physical orientation of the tire must be corrected. The noise will likely persist and potentially worsen until the tires are remounted with the correct directional bias on all four corners. Always verify the direction arrows on the sidewalls before and after any rotation service to ensure consistency across the entire vehicle.
